questions.question:
Assertion (A): The gas liberated on warming a salt with dil \(\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{SO}_4\), turns a piece of paper dipped in lead acetate into black, it is a confirmatory test for sulphide ion.

Reason (R): In statement-I the colour of paper turns black because of formation of lead sulphite.

 

[JEE Main 2024, 30 Jan (Shift 1)]
options: Assertion is true but the reason is false
Assertion is false but reason is true
Both assertion and reason are true and reason is the correct explanation of assertion
Both assertion and reason are true but reason is not the correct explanation of assertion
questions.explanation:
Assertion (A):

The gas liberated on warming a salt with dilute H₂SO₄ turns a piece of paper dipped in lead acetate black — confirmatory test for sulphide ion.

True.

When a sulphide salt (like FeS, ZnS, etc.) is treated with dilute H₂SO₄, hydrogen sulphide gas (H₂S) is evolved:

FeS + H2SO4 → FeSO4 + H2S↑

The evolved H₂S gas reacts with lead acetate paper to form black lead sulphide (PbS).

So this is indeed a confirmatory test for sulphide ion (S²⁻).

Reason (R):

The colour of paper turns black because of formation of lead sulphite.

False.

The black compound formed is lead sulphide (PbS), not lead sulphite (PbSO₃).

Correct Answer: A

Assertion is true but the reason is false.

Consider the system of linear equations \(x+y+z=4 \mu, x+2 y+2 \lambda z=10 \mu, x+3 y+4 \lambda^2 z=\mu^2+15\), where \(\lambda, \mu \in R\). Which one of the following statements is NOT correct?

 

[JEE Main 2024, 30 Jan (Shift 1)]
options: The system has unique solution if \(\lambda \neq \frac{1}{2}\) and \(\mu \neq 1,15\)
The system has infinite number of solutions if \(\lambda=\frac{1}{2}\) and \(\mu=15\)
questions.explanation:
Let \(D=\begin{vmatrix}
1&1&1\\
1&2&2\lambda\\
1&3&4\lambda^2
\end{vmatrix}\).

Then \(D=(2\lambda-1)^2\).

Hence, by Cramer's Rule, the system has a unique solution whenever

\(\lambda\neq\dfrac12\).

Therefore the only critical case is

\(\lambda=\dfrac12\).

the system becomes

\(x+y+z=4\mu\),

\(x+2y+z=10\mu\),

\(x+3y+z=\mu^2+15\).

\(D=0\).

Using Cramer's Rule, compute

\(D_1=\begin{vmatrix}
4\mu&1&1\\
10\mu&2&1\\
\mu^2+15&3&1
\end{vmatrix}\)

\(=4\mu(2-3)-(\,10\mu-\mu^2-15\,)+(30\mu-2\mu^2-30)\)

\(=-\mu^2+16\mu-15\)

\(=-(\mu-1)(\mu-15)\).

Similarly, \(D_2=\begin{vmatrix}
1&4\mu&1\\
1&10\mu&1\\
1&\mu^2+15&1
\end{vmatrix}\)

\(=\mu^2-16\mu+15\)

\(=(\mu-1)(\mu-15)\).

\(D_3=\begin{vmatrix}
1&1&4\mu\\
1&2&10\mu\\
1&3&\mu^2+15
\end{vmatrix}\)

\(=\mu^2-16\mu+15\)

\(=(\mu-1)(\mu-15)\).

\(D=D_1=D_2=D_3=0\)

\(\mu=1\)

\(\mu=15\).

Therefore the system has infinitely many solutions for

\(\lambda=\dfrac12,\ \mu=1\)

\(\lambda=\dfrac12,\ \mu=15\).

\(\lambda=\dfrac12\)

\(\mu\neq1,15\),

then at least one of \(D_1,D_2,D_3\) is non-zero while \(D=0\).

Hence the system is inconsistent.

Therefore for \(\lambda\neq\dfrac12\), the system has a unique solution;

for \(\lambda=\dfrac12,\ \mu=1\) or \(15\), it has infinitely many solutions;

for \(\lambda=\dfrac12,\ \mu\neq1,15\), it is inconsistent

Let \(g : R \rightarrow R\) be a non constant twice differentiable function such that \(g ^{\prime}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)= g ^{\prime}\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)\). If a real valued function \(f\) is defined as \(f(x)=\frac{1}{2}[g(x)+g(2-x)]\), then

 

[JEE Main 2024, 30 Jan (Shift 1)]
questions.explanation:
The function is \(f(x)=\dfrac12[g(x)+g(2-x)]\).

 \(f'(x)=\dfrac12[g'(x)-g'(2-x)]\).

At \(x=\dfrac12\), we have \(2-x=\dfrac32\).

Therefore, \(f'\left(\dfrac12\right)=\dfrac12\left[g'\left(\dfrac12\right)-g'\left(\dfrac32\right)\right]\).

Given \(g'\left(\dfrac12\right)=g'\left(\dfrac32\right)\),

this gives \(f'\left(\dfrac12\right)=0\).

At \(x=1\), we get

\(f'(1)=\dfrac12[g'(1)-g'(1)]=0\).

At \(x=\dfrac32\), we have

\(2-x=\dfrac12\).

Thus \(f'\left(\dfrac32\right)=\dfrac12\left[g'\left(\dfrac32\right)-g'\left(\dfrac12\right)\right]=0\).

Hence \(f'\) has three distinct zeros at \(\dfrac12,1,\dfrac32\).

By Rolle's theorem applied to \(f'\) on \(\left[\dfrac12,1\right]\),

there is at least one point in \(\left(\dfrac12,1\right)\) where \(f''(x)=0\).

Applying Rolle's theorem on \(\left[1,\dfrac32\right]\),

there is at least one point in \(\left(1,\dfrac32\right)\) where \(f''(x)=0\).

These two points are distinct.

Therefore, \(f''(x)=0\) for at least two values of \(x\) in \((0,2)\).

[JEE Main 2024, 30 Jan (Shift 1)]
questions.explanation:
Let \(L=\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{n^3}{(n^2+k^2)(n^2+3k^2)}\).

Divide numerator and denominator by \(n^4\), then

\( \frac{n^3}{(n^2+k^2)(n^2+3k^2)}=\frac{1}{n}\cdot\frac{1}{\left(1+\frac{k^2}{n^2}\right)\left(1+3\frac{k^2}{n^2}\right)} \).

So \(L=\int_0^1 \frac{dx}{(1+x^2)(1+3x^2)}\).

Now \( \frac{1}{(1+x^2)(1+3x^2)}=\frac{A}{1+x^2}+\frac{B}{1+3x^2} \).

Thus \(1=A(1+3x^2)+B(1+x^2)\).

Comparing coefficients, \(A+B=1\) and \(3A+B=0\).

On solving, \(A=-\frac{1}{2}\) and \(B=\frac{3}{2}\).

Therefore \(L=\int_0^1\left(-\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{1+x^2}+\frac{3}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{1+3x^2}\right)dx\).

So \(L=-\frac{1}{2}\left[\tan^{-1}x\right]_0^1+\frac{3}{2}\left[\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\tan^{-1}(\sqrt{3}x)\right]_0^1\).

Hence \(L=-\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{\pi}{4}+\frac{3}{2\sqrt{3}}\cdot\frac{\pi}{3}\).

So \(L=-\frac{\pi}{8}+\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi}{6}=\frac{(4\sqrt{3}-3)\pi}{24}\).

Now \( \frac{13\pi}{8(4\sqrt{3}+3)}=\frac{13\pi(4\sqrt{3}-3)}{8(48-9)}=\frac{(4\sqrt{3}-3)\pi}{24} \).

Therefore the required value is \( \frac{13\pi}{8(4\sqrt{3}+3)} \).

questions.question:
Let \(\alpha, \beta \in N\) be roots of the equation \(x^2-70 x+\lambda=0\), where \(\frac{\lambda}{2}, \frac{\lambda}{3} \notin N\). If \(\lambda\) assumes the minimum possible value, then \(\frac{(\sqrt{\alpha-1}+\sqrt{\beta-1})(\lambda+35)}{|\alpha-\beta|}\) is equal to :

 

[JEE Main 2024, 30 Jan (Shift 1)]
questions.explanation:
Since \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb N\) are roots,

\(\alpha+\beta=70\)

\(\alpha\beta=\lambda\)

Also,

\(\dfrac{\lambda}{2},\dfrac{\lambda}{3}\notin\mathbb N\)

so \(\lambda\) is divisible by neither \(2\) nor \(3\).

Let \(\alpha=n\). Then

\(\beta=70-n\)

and

\(\lambda=n(70-n)\)

To get the minimum possible value of \(\lambda\), we take the smallest positive \(n\) such that \(n(70-n)\) is divisible by neither \(2\) nor \(3\).

Since \(70\) is even, \(n(70-n)\) is odd only when both \(n\) and \(70-n\) are odd.

Trying odd values:

\(n=1\Rightarrow \lambda=69\), divisible by \(3\).

\(n=3\Rightarrow \lambda=201\), divisible by \(3\).

\(n=5\Rightarrow \lambda=325\), divisible by neither \(2\) nor \(3\).

Hence the minimum value is obtained for

\(\alpha=5,\quad \beta=65\)

and

\(\lambda=325\).

Now,

\(\sqrt{\alpha-1}+\sqrt{\beta-1}\)

\(=\sqrt4+\sqrt{64}\)

\(=2+8=10\)

Also,

\(\lambda+35=325+35=360\)

and

\(|\alpha-\beta|=|5-65|=60\)

Therefore,

\(\dfrac{(\sqrt{\alpha-1}+\sqrt{\beta-1})(\lambda+35)}{|\alpha-\beta|}\)

\(=\dfrac{10\times360}{60}\)

\(=60\)

Continuity at \(x=2\) requires \(4a+2b=\dfrac12\)

For \(x>2\), \(\displaystyle f(x)=\dfrac1x\),

so the right derivative at \(2\) is \(-\dfrac14\)

For \(|x|<2\), \(f'(x)=2ax\),

so the left derivative at \(2\) is \(4a\)

Differentiability gives \(4a=-\dfrac14\),

so \(a=-\dfrac1{16}\)

Using continuity,

\(-\dfrac14+2b=\dfrac12\)

Therefore, \(2b=\dfrac34\),

so, \(b=\dfrac38\)

At \(x=-2\), these same values also satisfy continuity and differentiability because

\(\dfrac1{|x|}=-\dfrac1x\)

for \(x<0\), whose derivative at \(-2\) is \(\dfrac14\), equal to \(-4a=\dfrac14\)

Thus,

\(a+b=-\dfrac1{16}+\dfrac38=\dfrac5{16}\)

Hence,

\(48(a+b)=48\cdot\dfrac5{16}=15\)

questions.question:
Number of integral terms in the expansion of \(\left\{7^{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}+11^{\left(\frac{1}{6}\right)}\right\}^{824}\) is equal to ____

 

[JEE Main 2024, 30 Jan (Shift 1)]
questions.explanation:
The general term in \(\left(7^{1/2}+11^{1/6}\right)^{824}\) is \(T_{r+1}=\binom{824}{r}7^{\frac{824-r}{2}}11^{\frac{r}{6}}\).

The binomial coefficient is always an integer.

Since \(7\) and \(11\) are different prime numbers, the term is an integer only when both exponents are integers.

Thus \(\dfrac{824-r}{2}\) must be an integer and \(\dfrac{r}{6}\) must be an integer.

The second condition gives \(r=0,6,12,\ldots\).

Every multiple of \(6\) is even, so \(824-r\) is also even.

Therefore, all multiples of \(6\) from \(0\) to \(824\) are valid.

The greatest such multiple is \(822=6\times 137\).

Hence the valid values are \(0,6,12,\ldots,822\).

The number of these values is \(137+1=138\).

Therefore, the number of integral terms is \(138\).

questions.question:

questions.explanation:
Let \(y=\sqrt{\frac{10x}{x+1}}\).

Since \(x\in[0,9]\), we have \(0\leq \frac{10x}{x+1}\leq9\).

So \(0\leq y\leq3\).

Hence \([y]\) can be \(0,1,2\), and value \(3\) occurs only at \(x=9\), which does not affect the integral.

For \([y]=0\), we need \(0\leq y<1\).

So \(0\leq \frac{10x}{x+1}<1\).

This gives \(0\leq x<\frac{1}{9}\).

For \([y]=1\), we need \(1\leq y<2\).

So \(1\leq \frac{10x}{x+1}<4\).

This gives \(\frac{1}{9}\leq x<\frac{2}{3}\).

For \([y]=2\), we need \(2\leq y<3\).

So \(4\leq \frac{10x}{x+1}<9\).

This gives \(\frac{2}{3}\leq x<9\).

Therefore \(\int_0^9\left[\sqrt{\frac{10x}{x+1}}\right]dx=0\cdot\left(\frac{1}{9}-0\right)+1\cdot\left(\frac{2}{3}-\frac{1}{9}\right)+2\cdot\left(9-\frac{2}{3}\right)\).

So \(\int_0^9\left[\sqrt{\frac{10x}{x+1}}\right]dx=\frac{5}{9}+2\cdot\frac{25}{3}\).

Thus \(\int_0^9\left[\sqrt{\frac{10x}{x+1}}\right]dx=\frac{5}{9}+\frac{50}{3}=\frac{155}{9}\).

Hence \(9\int_0^9\left[\sqrt{\frac{10x}{x+1}}\right]dx=9\cdot\frac{155}{9}=155\).

The differential equation is

Squaring,

\(\because b^2>0\)

Thus,

\(l=3,\ m=2,\ n=13\)

\(l^2+m^2+n^2=9+4+169=182\)

\(\therefore l^2+m^2+n^2=182\)
